name: Reporting to Families
title: Reporting to Families
answer: Reporting to Families means turning assessment data into plain-language progress reports that parents can understand and act on, delivered in time to help and in the family's own language. It matters because clear, timely messages about missed assignments, grades, and absences have been shown to reduce course failures and raise math scores, making families partners in a child's progress rather than spectators.

crumbs.name: Assessment, Data, and the Early Warning System

sections.body: Families need to know how their children are doing, and they need that information in language they can understand and early enough to make a difference. The problem is that raw data, such as a percentile score, tells most parents very little about what their child actually knows or needs. Family friendly progress reports solve this by explaining what the data means, for example naming a strength in fractions and a need for practice with word problems. AI can help convert data into these clear explanations, with the teacher checking the result. This puts assessment data to work in a form families can use.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school, progress reports are written to explain meaning rather than list numbers, so a parent learns what their child is strong in and where practice is needed. Student information system portals and messaging tools such as TalkingPoints can deliver these reports in the languages families speak. The translation rules from Chapter 14 apply, meaning critical information about a child's progress gets human review in the family's language. The text does not give separate grade band guidance for this idea. The teacher remains the one who checks the AI-generated explanations before they reach families.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels these findings as among the strongest in this Volume. Chapter 14 described trials in which weekly messages about missed assignments, grades, and absences cut course failures by 27 percent (Bergman et al., 2021) and raised math scores in Chile (Berlinski et al., 2021). These figures and studies are stated exactly as the text gives them.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: A report that only lists numbers, such as a percentile, leaves many parents without anything useful, so explanations must carry the meaning. AI can draft clear explanations, but the teacher checks them before they go out. Critical information about a child's progress deserves human review in the family's language, following the translation rules from Chapter 14. The decisions about what a child's progress means and what families should be told stay with people, not with the system.
